title: Heat and temperature (part 4)
textbookText: Consider two bodies A and B which are separated by non-conducting wall. Let both are separately connected with system C by conducting wall as shown in figure 9.4. If bodies are kept in such contact for sometimes, then body A and B separately exchange their heat with body C. Finally, both A and B separately attain thermal equilibrium with C. When adiabatic wall between A and B is replaced by diathermic wall and they are separated from C by adiabatic wall as in second figure, then A and B both exhibit no change in temperature. This indicates that A and B were already in thermal equilibrium. This verifies the Zeroth law of thermodynamics.
Physics, Grade 11 | 212

Long after the use of first and second law of thermodynamics Ralph Howard Fowler, in 1931, formulated this law for the very fundamental single valued function (temperature). Hence this law was labeled as Zeroth law of thermodynamics.

9.9 Thermometry
[ Fig.9.5, A thermometer]

Thermometry is the science of temperature and its measurement and the device used to measure the temperature is called thermometer. Working principle of thermometer is that the change in temperature brings some changes in measurable physical properties of a body. For example; change in,
i. Length of bar
ii. Volume of liquid
iii. Volume of gas at constant pressure
iv. Pressure of gas at constant volume
v. Magnetic properties of substance
vi. Electrical resistance of a wire, etc.

To measure the temperature of a body, the bulb of thermometer and object whose temperature is to be measured are brought in thermal contact and certain time is provided to bring them in thermal equilibrium. The main three steps of thermometry are: i. Construction ii. Calibration iii. Sensitiveness
Physics, Grade 11 | 213

[ Fig.9.6, Calibration of a thermometer] Construction: A thermometer is constructed in such a way that the uniform variation in properties of thermometric substance with temperature is maintained. Thermometric substances may be solid, liquid or gas, and must be highly sensitive toward temperature change. Calibration: While calibrating a thermometer, at first two standard degree of hotness (fixed points) are noted and then units are provided by dividing the interval between fixed points into different number of equal parts. The numbers of equal parts are different in different temperature scales.
Sensitiveness As far as possible thermometer should be more sensitive so that;
1. It can read the temperature of body immediately. 2. It does not exchange large amount of heat with the body whose temperature is to be
measured. It gives almost accurate reading. 3. It can read even a very small change in temperature.
Upper fixed point (UFP): It is the temperature at which pure water boils under standard atmospheric pressure.
Lower fixed point (LFP):It is the temperature at which pure ice melts under standard atmospheric pressure.

9.10 Absolute Scale and Absolute Zero Temperature: Temperatures expressed in Kelvin scale are absolute temperatures. The zero value of temperature in this scale is called absolute zero temperature. Absolute zero temperature is the lowest possible temperature which can exist in the universe. Temperature which is 273 divisions below the lower fixed point of Kelvin scale, and has value of –273.15°C is absolute zero temperature. At this temperature molecular motion stops and total kinetic energy of molecules becomes zero. It is highly condensed state of matter.
